title: Wet work on site: slurry, runoff and slip control
audience: Stone and terrazzo restoration technicians and site leads who run wet honing and polishing and who manage the floor, the drains and the public around the work
learningOutcomes: Explain why slurry is both a waste problem and a dust and slip hazard
Set up containment, collection and drain protection before the first pass
Clean slurry continuously with approved methods and manage wet floors
Respond to slurry that reaches a drain by stopping the water and containing the flow
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: SSROC/Woollahra, Concrete, brick and tile cutting (sheet 5) (no date shown); SWA, Working with silica and silica containing products (national guidance) (February 2022).

instruction.heading: Slurry is waste, dust and a slip hazard
instruction.body: Honing and polishing produce slurry, which is a mixture of water, stone particles and, where a chemical has been used, the chemical. The water keeps the silica dust in the slurry during the work, which is the point of the wet method. Once the slurry dries, however, the particles can become airborne dust again, and a wet floor left unmarked is a slip hazard. Slurry that flows into a drain, a gutter or stormwater can carry stone particles and chemicals into waterways. Council guidance for wet cutting says waste must be kept out of the stormwater network, because slurry can clog pipes and make the water more alkaline. Plan the handling of slurry with the site and the local rules before the first pass.

instruction.heading: Containment, collection and drain protection
instruction.body: Before the work starts, set up containment. Use barriers, slurry collection mats or a bunded area, and cover or block drains that the slurry could reach, using covers that are suited to the purpose. Where a wet vacuum is used for slurry, confirm that its rating and the manufacturer's instructions allow it for slurry, and do not use a general-purpose vacuum on dust. Collect solids from the containment and store them in a sealed container until disposal. Let settled slurry dry in a contained area only if the site rules allow it, and never sweep it dry. Council guidance says small quantities may be left in lined ditches to dry out, while larger volumes need a licensed recycler or landfill. Dispose of slurry by the site procedure and the state rules. Where settling tanks are used, keep the water and the solids apart as the site plan requires. Keep a clean path for workers and the public, and keep hoses and cords out of the walkway.

instruction.heading: Clean as you go and manage wet floors
instruction.body: Clean slurry as you go, not at the end of the day. Use low-pressure water, wet sweeping or the rated vacuum. Never use compressed air or dry sweeping. Mark the wet area with signs and cones, and manage access so that people do not walk through the slurry. Wear footwear with good grip, as set by the site induction. If the work cannot be made safe for the floor or the people around it, stop the work and make the area safe before resuming. If slurry reaches a drain, stop the water flow at once, contain the flow, tell the site manager and record the event. Follow the incident reporting procedure for the site.

procedure: Confirm the containment, collection and drain protection before the first pass.
Check the local and state slurry rules for the site, and note the disposal route.
Set up barriers, signs and cones to mark the wet area and manage access.
Keep the water flow controlled so that slurry stays inside the containment.
Clean slurry continuously with low-pressure water, wet sweeping or a rated vacuum.
If slurry reaches a drain, stop the water, contain the flow, notify the site manager and record the event.
At the end of the work, complete the final wet clean, dispose of collected slurry by the site procedure and record the disposal.

workedExamples.situation: Terrazzo polishing is underway in a shopping centre amenities area. Slurry is running towards a floor drain, and the crew has not set up a drain cover.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first action, and what happens next?
workedExamples.reasoning: The first action is to stop the water flow so that less slurry is produced, and then to contain the flow with a suitable barrier or cover on the drain. The crew then collects the slurry that has already moved, notifies the centre manager, and records the event under the incident procedure. The work does not restart until containment is set up and the drain is protected.

equipmentAndPpe: Slurry containment, collection mats, barriers and bunding
Drain covers suited to the drain and the purpose
Wet vacuum rated and approved for slurry, where used
Wet sweeping tools and low-pressure water equipment
Signs, cones and access controls for the wet area
Footwear and PPE set by the site induction

commonErrors.error: Letting slurry run towards a drain without containment.
commonErrors.prevention: Set up containment and drain protection before the first pass.

commonErrors.error: Leaving slurry to dry on the floor until the end of the day.
commonErrors.prevention: Clean as you go, and collect and contain the slurry continuously.

commonErrors.error: Dry sweeping slurry to speed up cleaning.
commonErrors.prevention: Use wet methods, low-pressure water or a rated vacuum. Dry sweeping is stop-work.
Mark and manage the wet area with signs and access control.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Check the state environment authority and the local council before the first pass; the council guidance cited here directs readers to their local council.

Stop-work rule: stop the water and the work if slurry reaches a drain and cannot be contained at once, or if the floor cannot be made safe for workers and the public. Record the event and follow the incident reporting procedure.
This lesson does not grant any permit or licence for discharge or waste handling.

qualityStandard: Containment and drain protection are in place before the first pass.
No slurry reaches a drain. Any that does is contained, reported and recorded.
The wet area is marked and the access is managed for the whole work period.
The floor is clean, dry and safe at handover.
documentationEvidence: Containment and drain protection record before start
Slurry disposal record with route and date
Incident record if slurry reached a drain or a person was affected
Final floor inspection record at handover
summary: Slurry is waste, a dust source once dry, and a slip hazard.
Contain the slurry and protect drains before the first pass.
Clean as you go with approved methods; never dry sweep or use compressed air.
If slurry reaches a drain, stop the water, contain it, report and record.
referencesAtEnd: Official sources to recheck before any job: SSROC/Woollahra, Concrete, brick and tile cutting (sheet 5) (no date shown); SWA, Working with silica and silica containing products (national guidance) (February 2022).

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the main concern with slurry from honing and polishing?
options: It is clean and harmless to the touch and the skin
It adds shine to the floor when it dries out fully
It can run into drains and dry into airborne dust
It is harmless once it is wet and spread out

knowledgeChecks.question: Which method is correct for cleaning up slurry?
options: Dry sweeping of the whole floor with a stiff broom and a dust pan
Compressed air blown across the whole floor and the walls nearby
Leaving it to dry overnight on the whole floor and the drain
A wet vacuum rated and approved for slurry, or contained collection

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should a wet area be marked?
options: To warn people and manage the slip risk
To increase the price of the job
For decoration only on the floor
To hide surface defects in the stone

knowledgeChecks.question: Slurry reaches a stormwater drain during the work. What is the first action?
options: Keep working and wash it away with the spray hose into the drain today
Stop the water flow, contain the flow, and report under the site and state rules
Wash it into the drain to clear it before the client sees the mess today
Ask the client what to do about the water and the drain on the day
